pp:me:2002:q31.detailed_solution:
In PERT (Program Evaluation and Review Technique), it is assumed that:

:

The project duration is governed by the critical path (the longest expected duration among all paths).

The project duration follows a normal distribution approximately, due to the Central Limit Theorem.

Step 1: List the mean durations and variances for each path:

Path 1: $\mu_1 = 10, \ \sigma_1^2 = 4$

Path 2: $\mu_2 = 12, \ \sigma_2^2 = 4$

Path 3: $\mu_3 = 12, \ \sigma_3^2 = 9$

Step 2: Identify the critical path

Since the critical path is the one with the maximum mean duration:

$\max(\mu_1, \mu_2, \mu_3) = \max(10, 12, 12) = 12$

We have two paths with mean duration 12.

As per PERT, among these, the path with the larger variance is considered for total project variance (more conservative estimate).

Thus, select Path 3:

$\mu = 12, \ \sigma^2 = 9$

Step 3: Write the distribution

The project duration approximately follows a normal distribution:

$N(\mu, \sigma^2)$

i.e.,

$N(12, 9)$

Or equivalently:

Mean = 12, Standard Deviation = $\sqrt{9} = 3$.

pp:me:2003:q20.detailed_solution:
From the observation of the T-s diagram of the rankine cycle, it reveals that heat is transferred to the working fluid during process 2-2' at a relatively low temperature. This lowers the average heat addition temperature and thus the cycle efficiency.

To remove this remedy, we look for the ways to raise the temperature of the liquid leaving the pump (called the feed water ) before it enters the boiler. One possibility is to transfer heat to the feed water from the expanding steam in a counter flow heat exchanger built into the turbine, that is, to use regeneration. A practical regeneration process in steam power plant is accomplished by extracting steam from the turbine at various points. This steam is used to heat the feed water and the device where the feed water is heated by regeneration is called feed water heater. So, regeneration improves cycle efficiency by increasing the average temperature of heat addition in the boiler.

pp:me:2004:q21.detailed_solution: Work output during the cycle $$\begin{aligned} &=m c_{p}\left(T_{3}-T_{2}\right)-m c_{p}\left(T_{4}-T_{1}\right) \\ &=m c_{p}\left(T_{3}-T_{4}\right)-m c_{p}\left(T_{2}-T_{1}\right) \\ &=m c_{p}\left[T_{3}\left(1-\frac{T_{4}}{T_{3}}\right)-T_{1}\left(\frac{T_{2}}{T_{1}}-1\right)\right] \end{aligned}$$ since $\frac{T_{3}}{T_{4}}=\frac{T_{2}}{T_{1}}=\left(r_{p}\right) \frac{\gamma-1}{\gamma} \quad\left(\text { Let } \frac{\gamma-1}{\gamma}=x, m c_{p}=K\right)$ $\therefore$ Work/cycle $=K\left[T_{3}\left(1-\frac{1}{r_{p}^{x}}\right)-T_{1}\left(r_{p}^{x}-1\right)\right]$ For maximum power, differentiate with respect to $r_{p}$ $$\begin{aligned} \Rightarrow \quad \frac{d W}{d r_{p}}&=K\left[T_{3} \times \frac{x}{r_{p}(x+1)}-T_{1} \times r_{p}^{(x-1)}\right]=0 \\ &\qquad (For max.)\\ \Rightarrow \frac{x T_{3}}{r_{p}(x+1)}&=T_{1} \times\left(r_{p}\right)^{x-1} \\ \Rightarrow \quad r_{p}^{2 x}&=\frac{T_{3}}{T_{1}} \\ \therefore \quad r_{p}&=\left(\frac{T_{3}}{T_{1}}\right)^{\frac{1}{2 x}} \\ \text{or }\quad r_{p}&=\left(\frac{T_{\max }}{T_{\min }}\right)^{\frac{\gamma}{2(\gamma-1)}} \end{aligned}$$

pp:me:2005:q79.detailed_solution: For Otto cycle $$\begin{array}{l} T_{1}=300 \mathrm{K} ; \quad T_{2}=450 \mathrm{K} \\ T_{3}=600 \mathrm{K} \end{array}$$ For process 1-2, $$\begin{aligned} \frac{T_{2}}{T_{1}}&=\left(\frac{V_{1}}{V_{2}}\right)^{\gamma-1}\\ \text{or}\quad \frac{V_{1}}{V_{2}} &=\left(\frac{T_{1}}{T_{2}}\right)^{\frac{\gamma}{\gamma-1}}=\left(\frac{450}{300}\right)^{\frac{1}{1.4-1}} \\ &=(1.25)^{2.5}=2.75 \end{aligned}$$ i.e., Compression ratio $$\begin{aligned} r&=\frac{V_{1}}{V_{2}}=2.75\\ \therefore \quad \eta_{\text {Otto }} &=1-\frac{1}{r^{\gamma-1}}=1-\frac{1}{(2.75)^{1.4-1}} \\ &=1-0.667=0.33=33 \% \end{aligned}\\ For Brayton cycle\\ \begin{aligned} T_{1}&=300 \mathrm{K} ; \quad T_{2}=450 \mathrm{K}\\ T_{3}&=550 \mathrm{K} \end{aligned}$$ For Brayton cycle $T_{1}=300 \mathrm{K} ; \quad T_{2}=450 \mathrm{K}\\ T_{3}=550 \mathrm{K}$ For process 1-2 Pressure ratio $$\begin{aligned} r_{p} &=\frac{p_{2}}{p_{1}}=\left(\frac{T_{2}}{T_{1}}\right)^{\frac{\gamma}{\gamma-1}} \\ \eta_{\text {Brayton }} &=1-\frac{1}{\left(r_{p}\right)^{\frac{\gamma-1}{\gamma}}} \\ &=1-\frac{1}{\left[\left(\frac{T_{2}}{T_{1}}\right)^{\frac{\gamma}{\gamma-1}}\right]^{\frac{\gamma-1}{\gamma}}} \\ &=1-\frac{1}{T_{1} / T_{2}}=1-\frac{T_{1}}{T_{2}}=1-\frac{300}{450} \\ &=0.33=33 \% \\ \text { Thus, } \eta_{\text {Otto }} &=\eta_{\text {Brajton }}=0.33 \end{aligned}$$

Mean $(\bar{t})=\int_{-1}^{\infty} t \cdot f(t) \cdot d t$

$\quad=\int_{-1}^{0} t(1+t) d t+\int_{0}^{1} t(1-t) d t$

$\quad=\left[\frac{t^{2}}{2}+\frac{t^{3}}{3}\right]_{-1}^{0}+\left[\frac{t^{2}}{2}-\frac{t^{3}}{3}\right]_{0}^{1}$

$\quad=-\left[\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{3}\right]+\left[\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{3}\right]$

$=-\left[\frac{1}{6}+\frac{1}{6}\right]=0$

Variance $=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}(t-\bar{t})^{2} f(t) d t$

$=\int_{-1}^{0} t^{2}(1+t) \cdot d t+\int_{0}^{1} t^{2}(1-t) d t$

$=\int_{-1}^{0}\left(t^{2}+t^{3}\right) \cdot d t+\int_{0}^{1} t^{2}(1-t) d t$

$=\left[\frac{t^{3}}{3}+\frac{t^{4}}{4}\right]_{-1}^{0}+\left[\frac{t^{3}}{3}-\frac{t^{4}}{4}\right]_{0}^{1}$

$=\frac{1}{12}+\frac{1}{12}=\frac{1}{6}$

Standard deviation

$=\sqrt{\text { variance }}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}$

pp:me:2007:q35.detailed_solution: Given, $$\begin{aligned} T_{i} &=21^{\circ} \mathrm{C} \\ T_{d p} &=10.17^{\circ} \mathrm{C} \\ T_{o} &=-23^{\circ} \mathrm{C} \\ h_{i} &=8 \mathrm{W} / \mathrm{m}^{2} \mathrm{K}, h_{o}=23 \mathrm{W} / \mathrm{m}^{2} \mathrm{K} \\ k &=1.2 \mathrm{W} / \mathrm{mK} \end{aligned}$$ The heat transfer rate per unit area in the slab can be calculated by considering convection at inner side. $$\begin{aligned} q &=h_{i}\left(T_{i}-T_{d p}\right) \\ &=8(21-10.17)=86.64 \mathrm{W} / \mathrm{m}^{2} \end{aligned}$$ Further this heat is conducted through wall $$\begin{aligned} \therefore q&=\frac{T_{d p}-T_{0}}{\frac{x}{k}+\frac{1}{h_{0}}}\\ 86.64 &=\frac{10.17-(-23)}{\frac{x}{1.2}+\frac{1}{23}}=\frac{33.17}{\frac{x}{1.2}+\frac{1}{23}} \\ \text { or } \frac{x}{1.2}+\frac{1}{23} &=\frac{33.17}{86.64}=0.3828 \\ \text { or }\quad \frac{x}{1.2} &=0.3393 \\ x &=1.2 \times 0.3393=0.4072 \mathrm{m} \end{aligned}$$

pp:me:2007:q36.detailed_solution: Given data: Mass flow rate of dry air $$\begin{aligned} m_{a}&=3 \mathrm{kg} / \mathrm{s} \\ h_{1}&=85 \mathrm{kJ} / \mathrm{kg} \text { of dry air } \\ \omega_{1}&=19 \mathrm{gm} / \mathrm{kg} \text { of dry air } \\ &=0.019 \mathrm{kg} / \mathrm{kg} \text { of dry air } \\ h_{2}&=43 \mathrm{kJ} / \mathrm{kg} \text { of dry air } \\ \omega_{2}&=8 \mathrm{gm} / \mathrm{kg} \text { of dry air } \\ &=0.008 \mathrm{kg} / \mathrm{kg} \text { of dry air } \end{aligned}$$ Enthalpy of condenrate water leaves the cooling $$\begin{aligned} \text { coil: } h_{f g}&=67 \mathrm{kJ} / \mathrm{kg} \\ \omega_{1}&=\frac{m_{v 1}}{m_{a}}\\ \text{or }\quad m_{v 1}&=\omega_{1} m_{a}=0.019 \times 3 \mathrm{kg} / \mathrm{s} \\ & =0.057 \mathrm{kg} / \mathrm{s}, \text{mass of water vapour at inlet} \\ \end{aligned}$$ Similarly, $m_{v 2}=\omega_{2} m_{a}=0.008 \times 3$ $=0.024 \mathrm{kg} / \mathrm{s},$ mass of water vapour at outlet Mass flow rate of condensate, $$\begin{aligned} m_{w} &=m_{v 1}+m_{v 2} \\ &=0.057+0.024=0.033 \mathrm{kg} / \mathrm{s} \end{aligned}$$ Cooling capacity of the coil, $$\begin{aligned} Q&=m\left(h_{1}-h_{2}\right)-m_{w} h_{f g}\\ \text{where }m\left(h_{1}-h_{2}\right)&= \text{sensible heat removed}\\ \therefore m_{w} h_{f g}&= \text{ Latent heat removed}\\ Q &=3(85-43)-0.033 \times 67 \\ &=123.79 \mathrm{kW} \end{aligned}$$ Alternatively Mass flow rate of condensate, $$\begin{aligned} m_{w} &=m_{a}\left(\omega_{1}-\omega_{2}\right) \\ &=3 \times(0.019-0.008) \\ &=0.033 \mathrm{kg} / \mathrm{s} \end{aligned}$$ Applying energy balance equation, we get $$\begin{aligned} m_{a} h_{1} &=m_{a} h_{2}+m_{w} h_{f g}+Q \\ 3 \times 85 &=3 \times 43+0.033 \times 67+Q \\ Q &=123.8 \mathrm{kW} \end{aligned}$$

pp:me:2007:q37.detailed_solution: $$\begin{aligned} Q_{1}+Q_{2} &=100 \mathrm{kJ} \\ T &=350 \mathrm{K} \\ T_{1} &=400 \mathrm{K} \\ T_{2} &=300 \mathrm{K} \end{aligned}$$ Entropy change of the heat temperature device: $$\begin{aligned} \Delta S &=-\frac{\left(Q_{1}+Q_{2}\right)}{350}=-\frac{100}{350} \\ &=-\frac{2}{7} \mathrm{kJ} / \mathrm{K} \end{aligned}$$ Entropy change of reservoir- 1 $\Delta S_{1}=\frac{Q_{2}}{T_{2}}=\frac{100-Q_{1}}{300} \mathrm{kJ} / \mathrm{K}$ Entropy change of reservoir- 2 $\Delta S_{2}=\frac{Q_{1}}{T_{1}}=\frac{Q_{1}}{400} \mathrm{kJ} / \mathrm{K}$ Total entropy $$\begin{aligned} \Delta S_{\text {total }} &=0 \\ \Delta S+\Delta S_{1}+\Delta S_{2} &=0 \\ -\frac{2}{7}+\frac{100-Q_{1}}{300}+\frac{Q_{1}}{400} &=0 \\ -\frac{2}{7}+\frac{1}{3}-\frac{Q_{1}}{300}+\frac{Q_{1}}{400} &=0 \\ -\frac{400 Q_{1}+300 Q_{1}}{120000}=\frac{2}{7}-\frac{1}{3} &=\frac{6-7}{21}=-\frac{1}{21} \\ -\frac{100 Q_{1}}{120000} &=-\frac{1}{21} \\ \text{or } \qquad Q_{1} &=57.14 \mathrm{kJ} \end{aligned}$$

pp:me:2007:q39.detailed_solution:
For steady, incompressible forced, vortex flow;

P. Shear stress in zero at all points in the flow. --Incorrect

Shear stress is always exit dut to external torque acting on mass of fluid.

Q.Vorticity is zero at all points in the flow.-- Incorrect

Velocity exists at all points in forced vortex flow field.

R. Velocity is directly proportional to the radius from the centre of the vortex. - Correct.

For forced vortex flow,

$\frac{V}{r}=\text { Constant }$

$\text{or }\quad V \propto r$

S. Total mechanical energy per unit mass is constant in the entire flow field. - Correct

$\frac{\rho \omega^{2}}{2}\left(r_{2}^{2}-r_{1}^{2}\right)-\rho g\left(z_{2}-z_{1}\right)=0$

$\text{or }\frac{\omega^{2}}{2}\left(r_{2}^{2}-r_{1}^{2}\right)-g\left(z_{2}-z_{1}\right)=0$

$\Delta \mathrm{K} . \mathrm{E} .-\Delta \mathrm{P.E.}=0$

where,

$\Delta K . E .=\frac{\omega^{2}}{2}\left(r_{2}^{2}-r_{1}^{2}\right)-\left(z_{2}-z_{1}\right)$

change in K.E. per unit mass

$\Delta P . E=g\left(z_{2}-z_{1}\right) \quad$

change in P.E. per unit mass

$\therefore \Delta K \cdot E .=\Delta P . E$

Hence, total mechanical energy per unit mass in constant.

pp:me:2007:q40.detailed_solution: Given: The flow is a steady incompressible forced vortex flow. Key property of forced vortex: $v = \omega r$ Evaluation of statements: P: Shear stress is zero at all points in the flow. In a forced vortex, the fluid rotates like a rigid body. There is no relative motion between adjacent fluid layers, hence no velocity gradient in the radial direction. $\therefore \text{Shear stress} = 0$ Statement P is TRUE. Q: Vorticity is zero at all points in the flow. For a forced vortex, vorticity is given by $\text{Vorticity} = 2\omega$ which is constant and non-zero. Statement Q is FALSE. R: Velocity is directly proportional to the radius from the centre of the vortex. From the forced vortex relation, $v = \omega r$ Velocity increases linearly with radius. Statement R is TRUE. S: Total mechanical energy per unit mass is constant in the entire flow field. In a forced vortex, pressure and kinetic energy vary with radius, so total mechanical energy is not constant throughout the flow field (it is constant only along a streamline). Statement S is FALSE.

pp:me:2009:q17.detailed_solution: Cold Shut: Two stream of liquid metal which are not hot enough to fuse properly result into a casting defect known as cold shut OR For a casting with gates at its two sides, the misrun may show up at the centre of the casting. When this happens, the defect is called a cold shut. Swell: This defect is found on the vertical surface of a casting if the moulding sand is deformed by the hydrostatic pressure caused by the high moisture content in the sand. Wash: A low projection on the drag surface of a casting commencing near the gate is called a wash. This is caused by erosion of sand due to the high velocity jet of liquid metal in bottom gating. Scab: This refers to the rough thin layer of a metal, protruding above the casting surface on the top of a thin layer of sand. The layer is held on the casting by a metal stringer through the sand. A scab results when the upheaved sand is separated from the mould surface and the liquid metal flows into the space between the mould and the displaced sand.

pp:me:2009:q20.detailed_solution:
Exponential smoothing methods of forecasting takes a fraction of forecast error into account for next period forecast

$$\begin{aligned} F_{t}&=F_{t-1}+\alpha\left(D_{t-1}-F_{t-1}\right) \\ F_{t}&=F_{t-1}+\alpha e_{t} \end{aligned}$$

where, $F_{t}$ is the forecast at time t

$D_{t}$ is the actual demand at time t

$F_{t-1}$ is the forecast at time t-1

$\alpha$ is the smoothing coefficient

$e_{t}=D_{t-1}-F_{t-1}$ is forecast error

The value of $\alpha$ varies between 0 and 1, with commonly used value of 0.01 to 0.30 .

New estimate = Old estimate of latest actual demand $+\alpha$ [latest actual demand - old estimate of latest actual demand]

Exponential smoothing provides a convenient, systematic and recursive method of revisiting the forecast for the next period whenever discrepancy exists between the previously forecast demand for current period and the actual demand for current period.

pp:me:2009:q24.detailed_solution: Let the point be the(x,y,z) The distance between two given coordinates is given as $$\begin{aligned} D^{2} &=\sqrt{(x-0)^{2}+(y-0)^{2}-(z-0)^{2}} \\ D^{2} &=x^{2}+y^{2}+z^{2} \\ \text { given } z^{2} &=1+x y \\ D^{2} &=x^{2}+y^{2}+1+x y \end{aligned}$$ Let $D^{2}=U$ $U=x^{2}+y^{2}+1+x y$ For minimum or nearest distance $$\begin{aligned} p &=\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}=0 \\ \Rightarrow 2x+y &=0 &... i \\ \Rightarrow \quad q &=\frac{\partial u}{\partial y}=0 \\ &=2y+x=0&... ii \end{aligned}$$ By solving equation (i) and (ii) $$\begin{aligned} &x=0\\ &y=0\\ &z=1\\ &\begin{aligned} r &=\frac{\partial^{2} v}{\partial x^{2}}=2 \\ t &=\frac{\partial^{2} v}{\partial y^{2}}=2 \\ s &=\frac{\partial^{2} u}{\partial x \partial y}=1 \\ r t-s^{2} &=2 \times 2-1^{2}=3 \\ r t-s^{2} &>0 \\r &>0 \end{aligned} \end{aligned}$$ $\therefore$ distance is minimum. pp:me:2009:q27.detailed_solution: Given data: $$\begin{aligned} d_{1}&=20 \mathrm{cm}=0.2 \mathrm{m} \\ d_{2}&=10 \mathrm{cm}=0.1 \mathrm{mm} \\ p_{1}&=150 \mathrm{kP} \mathrm{a}=150000 \mathrm{Pa} \end{aligned}$$ Vapour pressure, $p_{v}=50 \mathrm{kPa}$ Specific weight $w=5 \mathrm{kN} / \mathrm{m}^{3}=5000 \mathrm{N} / \mathrm{m}^{3}=\rho \mathrm{g}$ Applying continuity equation at section (1)-(1) and (2)-(2), we get $A_{1} V_{1}=A_{2} V_{2} \quad$ for incompressible flow $$\begin{aligned} \frac{\pi}{4} d_{1}^{2} V_{1} &=\frac{\pi}{4} d_{2}^{2} V_{2} \\ d_{1}^{2} V_{1} &=d_{2}^{2} V_{2}\\ or \quad V_{1}&=\left(\frac{d_{2}}{d_{1}}\right)^{2} V_{2}=\left(\frac{10}{20}\right)^{2} V_{2} \\ V_{1}&=0.25 \mathrm{V}_{2} \end{aligned}$$ The maximum pressure in downstream of reducer should be greater or equal to vapour pressure $\left(p_{v}\right)$ to avoid cavitation. Therefore for maximum discharge, $p_{2}=p_{v}=50 \mathrm{kPa}=50000 \mathrm{Pa}$ Applying Bernoulli's equation a section (1)-(1) and (2)-(2), we get $\frac{p_{1}}{\rho g}+\frac{V_{1}^{2}}{2 g}+z_{1}=\frac{p_{2}}{\rho g}+\frac{V_{2}^{2}}{2 g}+z_{2}$ $\frac{p_{1}}{\rho g}+\frac{V_{1}^{2}}{2 g}=\frac{p_{2}}{\rho g}+\frac{V_{2}^{2}}{2 g} \quad \because z_{1}=z_{2}$ $\frac{150000}{5000}+\frac{(0.25)^{2} V_{2}^{2}}{2 \times 9.81}=\frac{50000}{5000}+\frac{V_{2}^{2}}{2 \times 9.81}$ $30+0.00318 V_{2}^{2}=10+0.0509 V_{2}^{2}$ $V_{2}^{2}=418.51$ $\text{or }\quad V_{2}=20.45 \mathrm{m} / \mathrm{s}$ $\therefore \quad Q=A_{2} V_{2}=\frac{\pi}{4} d_{2}^{2} V_{2}$ $=\frac{3.14}{4} \times(0.1)^{2} \times 20.45=0.160 \mathrm{m}^{3} / \mathrm{s}$

pp:me:2009:q28.detailed_solution: $$\begin{aligned} T_{h 1}&=102^{\circ} \mathrm{C} \\ T_{c 1}&=15^{\circ} \mathrm{C} \\ m_{h}&=1 \mathrm{kg} / \mathrm{s} \\ c_{p h}&=4 \mathrm{kJ} / \mathrm{kgK} \end{aligned}$$ Overall heat transfer coefficient $U=1 \mathrm{kW} / \mathrm{m}^{2} \mathrm{K}$ Heat transfer surface area, $A=5 \mathrm{m}^{2}$ Given: $m_{c} c_{p c}=m_{h} c_{p h}=1 \times 4=4 \mathrm{kJ} / \mathrm{s} \mathrm{k}$ Neglect heat transfer between the heat exchanger and the ambient. The heat exchanger is characterized by the following relation[/latex] $$\begin{aligned} 2 \epsilon &=1-\exp (-2 N T U) \\ \text{or }\quad \in&=\frac{1-\exp (-2 N T U)}{2} \\ N T U &=\frac{U A}{C_{\min }} \\ &=\frac{1 \times 5}{4}=1.25 \\ \epsilon &=\frac{1-\exp (-2 N T U)}{2} \\ &=\frac{1-\exp (-2 \times 1.25)}{2}=0.46 \end{aligned}$$ The maximum possible heat transfer rate, $$\begin{aligned} Q_{\max } &=C_{\min }\left(T_{h 1}-T_{c 1}\right) \\ &=4 \times(102-15)=348 \mathrm{kW} \end{aligned}$$ Actual rate of heat transfer, $$\begin{aligned} Q &=\epsilon Q_{\max } \\ &=0.46 \times 348=160 \mathrm{kW}\\ \text{also }\quad Q&=C_{c}\left(T_{c 2}-T_{c 1}\right)\\ \therefore \quad 160&=4 \times\left(T_{\mathrm{c} 2}-15\right)\\ \text{or}\quad T_{c 2}&=55^{\circ} \mathrm{C}\\ \end{aligned}$$

pp:me:2009:q29.detailed_solution: Given data for Otto cycle: Compression ratio, $$\begin{aligned} r &=\frac{v_{1}}{v_{2}}=10 \\ p_{1} &=100 \mathrm{kPa} \\ T_{1} &=27^{\circ} \mathrm{C}=(27+273) \mathrm{K} \\ &=300 \mathrm{K} \\ q_{1} &=1500 \mathrm{kJ} / \mathrm{kg} \\ q_{2} &=700 \mathrm{kJ} / \mathrm{kg} \\ R &=0.287 \mathrm{kJ} / \mathrm{kgK} \\ p_{1} v_{1} &=R T_{1} \\ 100 \times v_{1} &=0.287 \times 300 \\ \text{or }\quad v_{1} &=0.861 \mathrm{m}^{3} / \mathrm{kg}\\ \text { also } \quad v_{1}&=10 v_{2} \\ \therefore \quad 0.861&=10 v_{2} \\ \text{or}\quad v_{2} &=0.0861 \mathrm{m}^{3} / \mathrm{kg} \end{aligned}$$ Specific work done per cycle, $$\begin{aligned} w &=q_{1}-q_{2} \\ &=1500-700=800 \mathrm{kJ} / \mathrm{kg} \end{aligned}$$ We know that mean effective pressure, $$\begin{aligned} p_{m} &=\frac{w}{v_{s}}=\frac{800}{v_{1}-v_{2}} \\ &=\frac{800}{0.861-0.0861}=1032.39 \mathrm{kPa} \end{aligned}$$

pp:me:2009:q30.detailed_solution: Given data: $$\begin{array}{ll} Q_{1}=100 \mathrm{kW} ; & Q_{2}=50 \mathrm{kW} \\ T_{3}=290 \mathrm{K} ; & T_{4}=348 \mathrm{K} \end{array}$$ Heat engine work output, $$\begin{aligned} W &=Q_{1}-Q_{2} \\ W &=100-50=50 \mathrm{kW} \\ &=\text { Pump input work } \\ (\mathrm{COP})_{\mathrm{HP}} &=\frac{Q_{4}}{W} \\ \text{also}(\mathrm{COP})_{\mathrm{HP}} &=\frac{T_{4}}{T_{4}-T_{3}} \\ \therefore \quad \frac{Q_{4}}{W} &=\frac{T_{4}}{T_{4}-T_{3}} \\ \frac{Q_{4}}{50} &=\frac{348}{348-290}=\frac{348}{58}\\ \text{or}\quad Q_{4}&=300 \mathrm{kW} \end{aligned}$$

pp:me:2009:q33.detailed_solution: Given data: $h_{1}=20 \mathrm{W} / \mathrm{m}^{2} \mathrm{K} ; \quad h_{0}=50 \mathrm{W} / \mathrm{m}^{2} \\ \mathrm{K} ; \quad T_{\infty^{\prime} 0}=20^{\circ} \mathrm{C} k_{1}=20 \mathrm{W} / \mathrm{mK} ; \quad k_{2}=50 \mathrm{W} / \mathrm{mK}$ $\mathrm{L}_{1}=0.30 \mathrm{m} ; \quad \mathrm{L}_{2}=0.15 \mathrm{m}$ Heat flow: $$\begin{aligned} Q &=\frac{T_{\infty, i}-T_{\infty, 0}}{R_{t_{i}}+R_{t_{1}}+R_{t_{2}}+R_{t_{o}}} \\ Q &=\frac{T_{\infty, i}-T_{\infty, 0}}{\frac{1}{h_{i} A}+\frac{L_{1}}{k_{1} A}+\frac{L_{2}}{k_{2} A}+\frac{1}{h_{o} A}} \\ \frac{Q}{A} &=\frac{T_{\infty, i}-T_{\infty, 0}}{\frac{1}{h_{i}}+\frac{L_{1}}{k_{1}}+\frac{L_{2}}{k_{2}}+\frac{1}{h_{0}}} \\ &=\frac{20-(-2)}{\frac{1}{20}+\frac{0.30}{20}+\frac{0.15}{50}+\frac{1}{50}} \\ &=\frac{20+2}{\frac{5+1.50+0.3+2}{100}}=\frac{22 \times 100}{8.8}=250 \mathrm{W} \\ \text{also}\qquad \frac{Q}{A}&= \frac{T_{\infty, 1}-T}{\frac{1}{h_{i}}+\frac{L_{1}}{k_{1}}}\\ \therefore \qquad 250&=\frac{20-T}{\frac{1}{20}+\frac{0.3}{20}}=\frac{20-T}{\frac{0.3}{20}}\\ 250 \times \frac{0.3}{20}&=20-T\\ 16.25&=20-T \\ \text{or }\quad T &=20-16.25 \\ &=3.75^{\circ} \mathrm{C} \end{aligned}$$

pp:me:2009:q34.detailed_solution: The velocity profile of a fully developed laminar flow in a straight circular pipe, as shown in figure, is given by the expression $$\begin{aligned} u(r) &=-\frac{R^{2}}{4 \mu}\left(\frac{d p}{d x}\right)\left[1-\frac{r^{2}}{R^{2}}\right] \\ &=U_{\max }\left[1-\frac{r^{2}}{R^{2}}\right] \\ \text { where } \quad U_{\max } &=-\frac{R^{2}}{4 \mu}\left(\frac{d p}{d x}\right) \end{aligned}$$ where $\frac{d p}{d x}$ is a constant The average velocity of fluid in the pipe, $V_{\mathrm{avg}}=\frac{U_{\max }}{2}=-\frac{R^{2}}{8 \mu}\left(\frac{d p}{d x}\right)$ Alternatively Given velocity profile expression, $u(r)=\frac{-R^{2}}{4 \mu}\left(\frac{d p}{d x}\right)\left[1-\frac{r^{2}}{R^{2}}\right]$ Consider a small circular ring element of radius r and thickness dr as shown in figure. The fluld flowing por socond through small elementaryring. dQ= Velocity at radius r x Area of a small ring element of a small $$\begin{aligned} &=u \times 2 \pi r d r \\ &=\frac{-1}{4 \mu} R^{2}\left(\frac{d p}{d x}\right)\left[1-\frac{r^{2}}{R^{2}}\right] \times 2 \pi r d r \\ &=\frac{-\pi}{2 \mu} R^{2}\left(\frac{d p}{d x}\right)\left[r-\frac{r^{3}}{R^{2}}\right] d r \end{aligned}$$ Net discharge flow through pipe, $$\begin{aligned} Q &=\int_{0}^{R} \frac{-\pi}{2 \mu} R^{2}\left(\frac{d p}{d x}\right)\left[r-\frac{r^{3}}{R^{2}}\right] d r \\ &=\frac{-\pi}{2 \mu} R^{2}\left(\frac{d p}{d x}\right) \int_{0}^{R}\left[r-\frac{r^{3}}{R^{2}}\right] d r \\ &=\frac{-\pi}{2 \mu} R^{2}\left(\frac{d p}{d x}\right)\left[\frac{r^{2}}{2}-\frac{r^{4}}{4 R^{2}}\right]^{A} \\ &=\frac{-\pi}{2 \mu} R^{2}\left(\frac{d p}{d x}\right)\left[\frac{R^{2}}{2}-\frac{R^{4}}{4 R^{2}}\right] \\ &=\frac{-\pi}{2 \mu} R^{2}\left(\frac{d p}{d x}\right)\left(\frac{R^{2}}{2}-\frac{R^{4}}{4}\right) \\ &=\frac{-\pi}{2 \mu} R^{2}\left(\frac{d p}{d x}\right) \times \frac{R^{2}}{4}=\frac{-\pi}{8 \mu} R^{4}\left(\frac{d p}{d x}\right)\end{aligned}$$ Average velocity, $$\begin{aligned}\bar{u} &=\frac{Q}{\pi R^{2}}=\frac{\overline{8} \mu}{\pi R^{2}}\left(\frac{d p}{d x}\right) \\ &=\frac{- R^{2}}{8 \mu}\left(\frac{d p}{d x}\right) \end{aligned}$$

pp:me:2009:q40.detailed_solution: For arm AB: At ant section X-X, at a distance x frome A $$\begin{aligned} M_{x} &=-P x \\ U_{A B} &=\int \frac{M_{x}^{2} d x}{2 E I}=\int_{0}^{L} \frac{(-P x)^{2}}{2 E I} d x \\ U_{A B} &=\frac{P^{2}}{2 E I}\left(\frac{x^{3}}{3}\right)_{0}^{L}=\frac{P^{2} L^{3}}{6 E I} \end{aligned}$$ For arm BC: $$\begin{aligned} R_{B}+R_{C} &=0 \\ M_{C} &=0 \\ R_{B} L-P L &=0 \\ R_{B} &=P \\ R_{C} &=-P \\ M_{x} &=R_{C} x=P_{x} \\ U_{B C} &=\int_{0}^{L} \frac{M_{x}^{2} d x}{2 E I}=\int_{0}^{L} \frac{P^{2} x^{2} d x}{2 E I} \\ &=\frac{P^{2} L^{3}}{6 E I} \end{aligned}$$ Total strain energy sotred in the frame of two arm $$\begin{array}{l} U=U_{A B}+U_{B C} \\ U=\frac{P^{2} L^{3}}{6 E I}+\frac{P^{2} L^{3}}{6 E I}=\frac{P^{2} L^{3}}{3 E I} \end{array}$$ Therefore, vertical deflection of A is $\delta_{A}=\frac{\partial U}{\partial P}=\frac{\partial}{\partial P}\left[\frac{P^{2} L^{3}}{3 E I}\right]=\frac{2 P L^{3}}{3 E I}$

pp:me:2009:q46.detailed_solution:
During orthogonal machining.

Shear strain: $\gamma=\cot \phi+\tan (\phi-\alpha)$

Cutting tool having rake angle: $\alpha=0^{\circ}$

then $\quad \gamma=\cot \phi+\tan \phi$

For minimum value of shea

$$\begin{aligned} \frac{d \gamma}{d \phi} &=\frac{d}{d \phi}(\cot \phi+\tan \phi)=0 \\ \frac{d \gamma}{d \phi} &=-\operatorname{cosec}^{2} \phi+\sec ^{2} \phi=0\\ -\frac{1}{\sin ^{2} \phi}+\frac{1}{\cos ^{2} \phi} &=0 \\ \Rightarrow \frac{\cos ^{2} \phi-\sin ^{2} \phi}{\cos ^{2} \phi \sin ^{2} \phi}&=0 \\ \Rightarrow \cos 2 \phi=0=\cos \frac{\pi}{2}&=\cos \frac{3 \pi}{2} \\ \Rightarrow \phi &= \frac{\pi}{4}\\ \frac{d^{2} \gamma}{d \phi^{2}}&=-2 \text{cosec} \phi \cdot(-\operatorname{cosec} \phi \cot \phi) \\ &+2\sec\phi.(\sec\phi\tan\phi)\\ \frac{d^{2} \gamma}{d \phi^{2}}&=2 \text{cosec}^{2} \phi \cot \phi+2 \sec ^{2} \phi\\ \left.\frac{d^{2} \gamma}{d \phi^{2}}\right|_{a+\phi=\frac{\pi}{4}}& \gt 0 \end{aligned}$$

Therefore $\gamma$ is minimum at $\phi=\frac{\pi}{4}$

Therefore minimum shear strain $\gamma$ is given by

$$\begin{aligned} \gamma &=\cot \frac{\pi}{4}+\tan \frac{\pi}{4} \\ &=2^{\circ} \end{aligned}$$

$\text{x=a, y=b is}$

$\text { Volume }=\int_{a}^{b} \pi y^{2} d x$

Here, $a=1, b=2$ and $y=\sqrt{x} \Rightarrow y^{2}=x$

$$\begin{aligned} \therefore Volume &=\int_{1}^{2} \pi \cdot x \cdot d x \\ &=\pi \cdot\left[\frac{x^{2}}{2}\right]_{1}^{2}=\frac{\pi}{2}\left[x^{2}\right]_{1}^{2} \\ &=\frac{\pi}{2}\left[2^{2}-1^{2}\right]=\frac{3}{2} \pi \end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned} y=|2-3 x| &=2-3 x \quad 2-3 x \geq 0 \\ &=3 x-2 \quad 2-3 x \lt 0 \end{aligned}$$

Therefore

$=3 x-2 \quad x \gt \frac{2}{3}$

since $2-3 x$ and $3 x-2$ are polynomials, these are continuous at all points. The only concern is at

$x=\frac{2}{3}$

Left limit at $x=\frac{2}{3} is 2-3 \times \frac{2}{3}=0$

Right limit at $x=\frac{2}{3} is 3 \times \frac{2}{3}-2=0$

$f\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)=2-3 \times \frac{2}{3}=0$

since, Left limit = Right limit $=f\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)$

Function is continuous at $\frac{2}{3}$

y is therefore continuous $\forall x \in R$

Now since $2-3 x$ and $3 x-2$ are polynomials,they are differentiable.

only concern is at $x =\frac{2}{3}$

Now, at $x=\frac{2}{3}$, L D= Left derivative =-3

R D= Right derivative =+3

$LD \neq RD$

$\therefore$ The function y is not differentiable at

$x=\frac{2}{3}$

If point B' is sufficiently far from B, these two forces (Gravity force and Buoyant force) create a restoring moment and return the body to the original position. A measure of stability for floating bodies is the metacentric height GM , which is the distance between the centre of gravity G and the metacenter M (the intersection point of the lines of action of the buoyant force through the body before and after rotation.) A floating body is stable if point M is above the point G, and thus GM is positive, and unstable if point M is below point G, and thus GM is negative. Stable equilibrium occurs when M is above G.

pp:me:2010:q25.detailed_solution:
Simplex method:

The simplex method is the most popular method used for the solution of Linear Programming Problems (LPP).

The Simplex method is a search procedure that shifts through the set of basic feasible solutions, one at a time until the optimal basic feasible solution is identified.

It can be used for two or more variables as well (always advisable for more than two variables to avoid lengthy graphical procedure).

The simplex method is not used to examine all the feasible solutions.

It deals only with a small and unique set of feasible solutions, the set of vertex points (i.e. extreme points/corner points) of the convex feasible space that contain the optimal solution.

All the resource values or constraints should be non-negative.

All the inequalities of the constraint should be converted to equalities with the help of slack or surplus variables.

Using the Double-Integration method to find out the deflection, given by

$0=\frac{12Pl^2}{Ebt^3}+C_1$

At  $x=l;\;\;y=0$

$0=\frac{12Pl}{Ebt^3}\times\frac{l^2}{2}-\frac{12Pl^2}{Ebt^3} l+C_2$

Let A be the event when student knows the answer and B be the event when student guesses the answer. Therefore

$P(A)=P(A\cap B)=\frac{2}{3}$

$P(B)=\frac{2}{3}+\frac{1}{3}\times \frac{1}{4}=\frac{9}{12}$

where $\frac{2}{3}$ is the probability of correct answer and $\frac{1}{3}$ is the probability that student does not know the answer. So guesses the answer and probability of correct guess is $\frac{1}{4}$. Therefore total probability of correct answer

$=\frac{2}{3}+\frac{1}{3} \times \frac{1}{4}=\frac{9}{12}$

Conditional probability that student knows the correct answer

pp:me:2013:q46.detailed_solution:
We have $\frac{\mathrm{d^{2}u} }{\mathrm{d} x^{2}}-k\frac{\mathrm{du} }{\mathrm{d} x}=0$

$(D^2-kD)u=0$

The auxiliary equation is

$$\begin{aligned} m^2-km&=0\\ m(m-k)&=0\\ m&=0,k \end{aligned}$$

Thus the complete solution is

$$\begin{aligned} u&=C_1e^{0x}+C_2e^{kx}\\ u&=C_1+C_2e^{kx} \end{aligned}$$

From given condition

$u(0)=0:\;\; C_1+C_2=0 \;\;\;...(i)$

$u(L)=U:\;\; U=C_1+C_2e^{kL}\;\;\;...(ii)$

Subtracting equation (i) from (ii), we get

$U=C_2(e^{kL}-1)$

$C_2=\frac{U}{e^{kL}-1}$

From equation (i), we have

$C_1=-C_2=\frac{-U}{e^{kL}-1}$

Substitute these values in the expression for u, we get

$u=\frac{-U}{e^{kL}-1}+\frac{U}{e^{kL}-1}e^{kx}=U\left ( \frac{1-e^{kx}}{1-e^{kL}} \right )$

$$=\left[\begin{array}{ll}-2 & 2 \\-9 & 9\end{array}\right]\left[\begin{array}{l}x \\y \end{array}\right]=0$$

pp:me:2015:q19.detailed_solution:
When a component is subjected to fluctuating stresses there is mean stress $(\sigma _m)$ as well as stress amplitude $(\sigma _a)$. It has been observed that the mean stress component has an effect on fatigue failure when it is present in combination with an alternating component.

When the component is subjected to both component of stress $(\sigma _m)$ and $(\sigma _a)$ the actual failure occurs at different scattered points as shown in figure. There exist a border which decides sole region from unsole region for various combinations of $(\sigma _m)$ and $(\sigma _a)$ and different criterion are proposed to constant the borderline dividing safe zone and failure zone, they include Gerber line, soderberg line, Goodman line, ASME elliptic.

Gerber Line:

A parabolic curve jointing $\sigma _e$ on the ordinate to $\sigma _{ut}$ on the abscissa is called Gerber line. It is written as

$\left (\frac{\sigma _a}{\sigma _e} \right )+\left (\frac{\sigma _m}{\sigma _{ut}} \right )^2=1$

Soderberg Line:

A straight line joining $\sigma _e$ on the ordinate to $\sigma _{yt}$ on the abscissa is called soderberg line. It is written as

$\left (\frac{\sigma _a}{\sigma _e} \right )+\left (\frac{\sigma _m}{\sigma _{yt}} \right )=1$

Goodman Line:

A straight line joining $\sigma _e$ on the ordinate to $\sigma _{ut}$ on the abscissa is called the Goodman line. It is written as

$\left (\frac{\sigma _a}{\sigma _e} \right )+\left (\frac{\sigma _m}{\sigma _{ut}} \right )=1$

ASME Elliptic:

The ASME elliptic is written as

$\left (\frac{\sigma _a}{\sigma _e} \right )^2+\left (\frac{\sigma _m}{\sigma _{yt}} \right )^2=1$

The soderberg line is a more conservative failure criterion and there is no need to consider even yielding in this case.

pp:me:2015:q24.detailed_solution:
In Linear arc welding process the heat input per unit length depends on many factors.

(A) Welding current:

As welding current increase as heat input increases because we know that heat input is $I^2RT$ so

$(\text{Heat input per unit length})\propto ( \text{current} )^2$

(B) Welding Voltage:

As welding voltage increase as heat input also increase because we know that heat input is $\frac{V^2}{R}$

$(\text{Heat input per unit length})\propto ( \text{voltage} )^2$

(C) Welding Speed:

As welding speed increase as welding electrode spend less time to release heat so as speed increase as heat input per unit length decrease proportionaly

$(\text{Heat input per unit length})\propto \frac{1}{( \text{welding speed} )}$

(D) Duty cycle:

Duty cycle is defined as the % of time for which arc is on without overheating element of welding machine so

$(\text{Heat input per unit length})\propto ( \text{duty cycle} )$

A generative manufacturing process different from a traditional manufacturing process develops a product with the addition of material instead of removal of the excess material as in case of a traditional manufacturing process.

In the generative manufacturing process, plans are generated by means of decision logic, formulas, technology algorithm and geometry-based data to perform uniquely the many processing decision for converting a part from raw material to a finished state.

There are two major components of a generative process planning system.

A geometry-based coding scheme.

Process knowledge in the form of decision logic and data.

The objective of a geometric based coding scheme is to define all geometric features for all process related surfaces together with feature dimensions, locations, tolerances and the surface finish desired on the features.

Advantage of Generative Manufacturing Process:

No tools and fixtures are required.

No restriction on geometry of the part shape exists.

Composite parts and assemblies can be produced in one go.

Small batch production of complex parts is economically viable.

pp:me:2016:q17.detailed_solution:
For stoichiometric burning (i.e., chemically correct),

number of moles of $\mathrm{O}_{2}$ required =5.

As it si burnt with 10 % deficient \mathrm{O}_{2} , it will generate CO.

That is, the new equation is

$\mathrm{C}_{3} \mathrm{H}_{8}+0.9 \times 5 \mathrm{O}_{2} \rightarrow \alpha \mathrm{CO}_{2}+\beta \mathrm{CO}+\gamma \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}$

Balancing carbon atoms, we get

$3=\alpha+\beta \quad \cdots(i)$

Balancing hydrogen atoms, we get

$$\begin{aligned} 8&=2 \gamma\\ \text{or }\quad \gamma&=4\\ \end{aligned}$$

Balancing oxygen atoms, we get

$$\begin{aligned} 0.9 \times 10 &=2 \alpha+\beta+\gamma \\ 9 &=2 \alpha+\beta+4 \\ 5 &=2 \alpha+\beta\quad \cdots(ii) \end{aligned}$$

Eq. (ii) - Eq. (i), we get

$$\begin{aligned} 2&=\alpha\\ \text{or }\quad \alpha&=2 \end{aligned}$$

$\mathrm{C}_{3} \mathrm{H}_{8}+\mathrm{aO}_{2} \rightarrow \mathrm{bCO}_{2}+\mathrm{cH}_{2} \mathrm{O}$

Balancing carbon atoms, we get

$$\begin{aligned} 3&=b\\ \text{or } \quad b&=3\\ \end{aligned}$$

Balancing hydrogen atoms, we get

$$\begin{aligned} 8&=2 c\\ \text{or}\quad c&=4\\ \end{aligned}$$

Balancing oxygen atoms, we get

$$\begin{aligned} 2 a &=2 b+c \\ 2 a &=2 \times 3+4=10 \\ a &=5 \end{aligned}$$

Substituting $\alpha=2$ in Eq. (ii), we get

$$\begin{array}{l} \quad 5=2 \times 2 \times \beta \\ \text { or } \quad \beta=1 \\ \therefore \mathrm{C}_{3} \mathrm{H}_{8}+4.5 \mathrm{O}_{2} \rightarrow 4 \mathrm{CO}_{2}+\mathrm{CO}+4 \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O} \end{array}$$

The volume percentage of CO in the product

$$\begin{array}{l} =\left(\frac{\beta}{\alpha+\beta+\gamma}\right) \times 100 \\ =\left(\frac{1}{2+1+4}\right) \times 100 \\ =14.28 \% \end{array}$$

pp:me:2016:q21.detailed_solution:
In welding, the two metals (or thermoplastic) must be similar. For example, copper cannot be welded to steel. Welding uses high temperatures to melt and join two metal parts. A filler metal is often used as well. When properly done, the finished weld is as strong as the surrounding metal.

Brazing joins two metals by heating and melting a filler (alloy) that bonds to the two pieces of metal and joins them. The filler obviously must have a melting temperature below that of the metal pieces. Brazing can join dissimilar metals such as aluminum, silver, copper, gold, and nickel.

Soldering  is a low-temperature analog to brazing. By the American Welding Society’s definition, soldering takes place with fillers (also known as solders) that melt at below $840^{\circ}F (450^{\circ}C)$. Metals that can be soldered include gold, silver, copper, brass, and iron. The filler, called solder, melts. When it solidifies, it is bonded to the metal parts and joins them. The bond is not as strong as brazed joint or welded one. Solder was once made mainly of lead, but environmental concerns are pushing industry to lead-free alternatives.

pp:me:2016:q37.detailed_solution: Total energy of system $$\begin{array}{l} \Rightarrow \frac{1}{2} M v^{2}+\frac{1}{2} K x^{2}+\frac{1}{2} I \omega^{2} \\ \Rightarrow \frac{1}{2} M \times\left(a \times \frac{d \theta}{d t}\right)^{2}+\frac{1}{2} K \times \\ \qquad \{(a+d) \theta\}^{2}+\frac{1}{2} \times \frac{M a^{2}}{2} \times\left(\frac{d \theta}{d t}\right)^{2}\\ \text{Let}\qquad \frac{d \theta}{d t}=\dot{\theta} \\ E=\frac{1}{2} M a^{2} \dot{\theta}^{2}+\frac{K}{2}(a+d)^{2} \cdot \theta^{2}+\frac{M a^{2}}{4} \dot{\theta}^{2} \end{array}$$ since energy of system remains concerned with respect to time. $$\begin{aligned} \frac{d E}{d t}&=0 \\ \frac{d E}{d t}&=\frac{M a^{2}}{2} 2 \cdot \dot{\theta} \cdot \ddot{\theta}+\frac{K}{2}(a+d)^{2} \\ & \qquad \cdot 2 \theta \cdot \dot{\theta}+\frac{M a^{2}}{4} \cdot 2 \dot{\theta} \ddot{\theta} \end{aligned}$$ $0=M a^{2} \dot{\theta} \ddot{\theta}+\frac{\lt a^{2}}{2} \cdot \dot{\theta} \ddot{\theta}+K(a+d)^{2} \theta \cdot \dot{\theta}$ Divide both sides by $\dot{\theta}$ $$\begin{aligned} 0&=M a^{2} \ddot{\theta}+\frac{M a^{2}}{2} \cdot \ddot{\theta}+K(a+d)^{2} \cdot \theta \\ 0&=\left(M a^{2}+\frac{M a^{2}}{2}\right) \ddot{\theta}+K(a+d)^{2} \theta \\ 0&=\frac{3}{2} M a^{2} \cdot \ddot{\theta}+K(a+d)^{2} \theta \end{aligned}$$ Divide both sides by $\frac{3}{2} m a^{2}$ $0=\ddot{\theta}+\frac{K(a+d)^{2}}{\frac{3 M a^{2}}{2}} \theta$ $\ddot{\theta}+\omega_{n}^{2} \theta=0$ Compairing above two equation $\omega_{n}^{2}=\frac{2 K(a+d)^{2}}{3 M a^{2}} ; \omega_{n}=\sqrt{\frac{2 K(a+d)^{2}}{3 M a^{2}}}$

pp:me:2016:q49-s2.detailed_solution:
Ratio of volume of pattern to volume of casting is given by

$=\frac{(1.03\times100)\times(1.03\times50)\times(1.03\times10)}{100\times50\times10}=1.093$

Volume of cavity is assumed to be small and negligible as it will complicate the question to a higher level.

If your answer was less than 1, read below.

There are three things to be understood here :-

1. Liquid Shrinkage

It refers to the reduction in volume when the metal changes from liquid state to solid state at the solidus temperature. The liquid shrinkage is rarely a problem, because the molten metal is continuously flowing in mold cavity and also riser to compensate the shrinkage of liquid in the cavity.

2. Solidification i.e Liquid to solid phase transformation (GCI expands in this process unlike other metals)

So now during phase transformation gray cast iron expands (unlike other metals which contract) and there is no need of riser (used to take care of phase transformation shrinkage + liquid shrinkage).

3. Solid state Cooling (GCI contracts in this process just like other metals)

It refers to the reduction in volume caused when metal loses temperature in solid state. To account for this, shrinkage allowance is provided on the patterns. The Shrinkage allowance depends primarily upon Coefficient of thermal expansion. For Grey CI in particular it is positive, it means solid grey cast iron expands on increasing temp and contracts on decreasing temperature just like any other metal.

Adding all above factors

Neglecting the Liquid shrinkage we see that GCI expands in during solidification and contracts when cooled in solid form. So the net result would be sum of them. According to NPTL in the table for GCI they have given the net value of shrinkage’s which is positive and hence the pattern size would be more than the casting.

Note: The expansion of GCI during phase change (solidification) is a fact but at the same time we need to consider the contraction of GCI when cooling in solid state. So net result according to IISC and NPTEL is contraction so the size of pattern will be more than that of casting.

pp:me:2016:q22-s3.detailed_solution: In a wire-cut EDM process, a thin metallic wire is fed on to the conducting workpiece, which is submerged in a tank of dielectric fluid such as de-ionized water. Wire is fed in the programmed path & material is cut from the workpiece accordingly. Material removal takes place by a series of discrete discharges between the wire electrode & workpiece in the presence of a dielectric fluid. The di-electric fluid gets ionized in between the tool electrode gap thereby creating a  path for each discharge. The area wherein discharge takes place gets heated to very high temperature such that the surface get melted & removed. The cut particles (debris) get flushed away by continuous flowing dielectric fluid. Generally, wire-cut EDM is used for cutting Aluminium, brass, etc. & wire material used for quicker cutting action is zinc coated brass wires.

2D incompressible flow continuity equation.

Given, 2-D incompressible frictionless fluid flow.

$\overrightarrow{\mathrm{u}}=x \hat{\mathrm{i}}-y \hat{\mathrm{j}}$

Thus, velocity components in  x  and  y  directions are :

$\mathrm{u}=\mathrm{x} \text { and } \mathrm{v}=-\mathrm{y}$

Navier-Stokes equation for incompressible, frictionless fluid flow reduces to

$\rho \frac{\mathrm{DV}}{\mathrm{Dt}}=-\nabla

\overrightarrow{\mathrm{P}}+\overrightarrow{\rho \mathrm{g}}$

There are no components of body force in  x  and  y  direction. Hence,

$\rho \frac{\mathrm{D} \overrightarrow{\mathrm{V}}}{\mathrm{Dt}}=-\nabla \overrightarrow{\mathrm{P}}$

where,  $\nabla \overrightarrow{\mathrm{P}}$  is the pressure gradient vector

Hence,

$$\begin{aligned} \bigtriangledown \vec{P}&=\rho \left [ \left ( u\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}+v\frac{\partial u}{\partial y} \right )\hat{i}+\left ( u\frac{\partial v}{\partial x} +v\frac{\partial v}{\partial y}\right ) \hat{j}\right ]\\ &=-\rho \left [ \{ x(1)+(-y)(0)\}\hat{i}+\{ x(0)+(-y)(-1)\} \hat{j}\right ]\\ &=-\rho (x\hat{i}+y\hat{j}) \end{aligned}$$

On the basis of nature of carbon present in cast iron, it may be divided into white cast iron and gray cast iron.

In the gray cast iron, carbon is present in free form as graphite. Under very slow rate of cooling during solidification, carbon atoms get sufficient time to separate out in pure form as graphite. In white cast iron, carbon is present in the form of combined form as cementite. In normal conditions, carbon has a tendency to combine with iron to form cementite.

pp:me:2021:q5-s2.detailed_solution:
Particle Size, Shape, and Distribution:

Particle size is generally controlled by screening, that is, by passing the metal powder through screens (sieves) of various mesh sizes. Several other methods also are available for particle-size analysis:

1. Sedimentation, which involves measuring the rate at which particles settle in a fluid.

2. Microscopic analysis, which may include the use of transmission and scanning- electron microscopy.

3. Light scattering from a laser that illuminates a sample, consisting of particles suspended in a liquid medium; the particles cause the light to be scattered, and a detector then digitizes the signals and computes the particle-size distribution.

4. Optical methods, such as particles blocking a beam of light, in which the particle is sensed by a photocell.

5. Suspending particles in a liquid and detecting particle size and distribution by electrical sensors.

pp:me:2021:q6-s2.detailed_solution: In contouring systems the machining path is usually constructed from a combination of linear and circular segments. It is only necessary to specify the coordinates of the initial and final points of each segment, and the feed rate. The operation of producing the required shape based on this information is termed interpolation and the corresponding unit is the "interpolator". The interpolator coordinates the motion along the machine axes, which are separately driven, by providing reference positions instant by instant for the position-and velocity control loops, to generate the required machining path. Typical interpolators are capable of generating linear and circular paths.

pp:me:2021:q7-s2.detailed_solution: Laser beam machining (LBM) is a nonconventional machining process,   which   broadly   refers   to the process of material removal, accomplished through the interactions between the laser and target materials. The processes can include laser drilling, cutting, grooving, writing, scribing, ablation, welding, cladding, milling, and so on. LBM is a thermal process, and unlike conventional mechanical processes, LBM removes material without mechanical engagement. In general, the workpiece is heated to melting or boiling point and removed by melt ejection, vaporization, or ablation.

pp:me:2022:q19.detailed_solution:
Surface Treatments:

During machining operations,small scratches

and grooves are invariably introduced into the

workpiece surface by cutting tool action. These

surface markings can limit the fatigue life. It has

been observed that improving the surface finish by

polishing will enhance fatigue life significantly.

One of the most effective methods of increasing

fatigue performance is by imposing residual

compressive stresses within a thin outer surface

layer. Thus, a surface tensile stress of external

origin will be partially nullified and reduced in

magnitude by the residual compressive stress. The

net effect is that the likelihood of crack formation

and therefore of fatigue failure is reduced.

Residual compressive stresses are commonly

introduced into ductile metals mechanically by

localized plastic deformation within the outer

surface region. Commercially, this is often

accomplished by a process termed shot peening.

Small, hard particles (shot) having diameters

within the range of 0.1 to 1.0 mm are projected at

high velocities onto the surface to be treated. The

resulting deformation induces compressive stresses

to a depth of between one-quarter and one-half of

the shot diameter.

Tensile Strength: The tensile strength, or ultimate

tensile strength (UTS), is the maximum load

obtained in a tensile test, divided by the original

cross-sectional area of the specimen.

where, $\sigma _u=$ Ultimate tensile strength, $kg/mm^2$

$P_{max}=$  Maximum load obtained in a tensile test, kg

$A_o=$  Original cross-sectional area of gauge length

of the test piece, $mm^2$

The tensile strength is a very familiar property and

widely used for identification of a material. It is

very easy to determine and is a quite reproducible

property. It is used for the purposes of specifications

and for quality control of a product. Tensile strength

can be empirically correlated to other properties

such as hardness and fatigue strength. For brittle

materials, the tensile strength is a valid criterion for

design.

pp:me:2022:q12-s2.detailed_solution:
Chain and Sprocket mechanism is not used in CNC

Machines.

Linear Motors Recently linear motors are being

increasingly considered for use in high performance

CNC machine tools. The linear motor consists of

a series of magnets attached to the machine base

and a set of electrical coils potted around a steel

laminate core attached to the moving slide.

The fact that there are no mechanical parts in contact

means that there is no wear periodic maintenance

required. Linear motors are not limited in travel

like ball screws. Larger bare required to achieve

high velocity, with a longer travel to prevent undue

vibration.

This larger ball screw results in a higher inertia. This

means a larger motor with more torque is required

(introduction inertia) and the responsiveness and

bandwidth of the system is reduced, resulting in

poor servo performance.

Machines built with linear motors and all-digital

drive systems can produce parts with higher

accuracy and tighter tolerances at higher feeds

and speeds. Also, they reduce significantly the

non-machining time with high acceleration and

deceleration rates.

pp:me:2022:q53-s2.detailed_solution:
General Heat conduction equation in Cartesian

coordinates is

$\frac{\partial }{\partial x}\left ( K_x\frac{\partial T}{\partial x} \right )+\frac{\partial }{\partial y}\left ( K_y\frac{\partial T}{\partial y} \right )\frac{\partial }{\partial z}\left ( K_z\frac{\partial T}{\partial z} \right )+q_g=\rho c\frac{\partial T}{\partial t}$

For one dimensional steady state heat generation

with variable thermal conductivity, the above

equation can be written as

$$\begin{aligned}

\frac{\partial }{\partial x}\left ( CT\frac{\partial T}{\partial x} \right )+q_g&=0\\

C\frac{\partial }{\partial x}\left ( T\frac{\partial T}{\partial x} \right )+q_g&=0\\

\frac{\partial }{\partial x}\left ( T\frac{\partial T}{\partial x} \right )+\frac{q_g}{C}&=0\\

\frac{\partial }{\partial x}\left ( T\frac{\partial T}{\partial x} \right )&=-\frac{q_g}{C}\\

\int \frac{\partial }{\partial x}\left ( T\frac{\partial T}{\partial x} \right )&=-\int \frac{q_g}{C}\\

\text{For 1-D heat flow}\\

\frac{\partial T}{\partial x}&=\frac{dT }{\partial x}\\

T\frac{dT}{dx}&=-\frac{q_gx}{C}+C_1\\

x=0\;\;\frac{dT}{dx}&=0\;\;C_1=0 \text{ (At centerline)}\\

T\frac{dT}{dx}&=-\frac{q_gx}{C}\\

\int TdT&=\int -\frac{q_gx}{C}dx\\

\frac{T^2}{2}&=\frac{-q_gx^2}{2C}+C_2 . . . (1)\\

T=T_s&=\text{Outside surface temperature}\\

\frac{T_S^2}{2}&=\frac{-q_gL^2}{2C}+C_2\\

C_2&=\frac{T-s^2}{2}+\frac{q_gL^2}{2C}\\

\text{Put }&c_2 \text{ in equation (1)}\\

\frac{T^2}{2}&=\frac{-q_ax^2}{2C}+\frac{T_s^2}{2}+\frac{q_gL^2}{2C}\\

\text{At }&x=0,T=T_{max}\\

\frac{T_{max}^2}{2}&=\frac{T_s^2}{2}+\frac{q_gL^2}{2C}\\

\frac{T_{max}^2}{2}&=\frac{600^2}{2}+\frac{128010^3 \times 1^2}{2 \times 2}\\

T_{max}&=1000K

\end{aligned}$$

pp:me:2023:q13.detailed_solution:
Soldering is define as a metal joining process

wherein coalescence is produced by heating the

surface to be joint to a suitable temperature and

melting the filler metal which is a fusible alloy called

solder (melting point usually less than $427^{\circ}C$

).

Principle underlying soldering is that when the

surface to be jointed are cleaned off well from

oxides they can be joined together using molten

solder that may adhere easily with the workpiece.

Brazing is also one of the type of welding process

which is used for joining the two similar or dissimilar

metal piece together by heating the surface and

by using a non-ferrous filler metal having its melting

point above $427^{\circ}C$ but below the melting point of

metal to be brazed. The molten filler metal is

$$\begin{aligned}

& y=x^{n} \\

& x^{2}(n)(n-1) x^{n-2}+x\left(n x^{n-1}\right)-x^{n}=0 \\

& x^{n}[x(n-1)+n-1)=0 \\

& n^{2}-1=0 \\

& n=\pm 1 \\

& y_{1}=x \\

& y_{2}=\frac{1}{x} \\

& y=C_{1} x+\frac{C_{2}}{x}

\end{aligned}$$

x & =1

$\Rightarrow \quad \frac{d y}{d t}=-2 y$

and step size, $\mathrm{h}=\Delta \mathrm{t}$

$\therefore \quad y_{n+1}=y_{n}+\Delta t\left(-2 y_{n}\right)$

$\mathrm{y}_{\mathrm{n}+1}=\mathrm{y}_{\mathrm{n}}(1-2 \Delta \mathrm{t})$

$\frac{y_{n+1}}{y_{n}}=1-2 \Delta t \;\;\;...(i)$

Given:

$\left|y_{n+1}\right| \leq\left|y_{n}\right|$

$\Rightarrow \quad\left|\frac{y_{n+1}}{y_{n}}\right| \leq 1$

From equation (i)

$\therefore \quad|1-2 \Delta t| \leq 1$

Case (i) when $(1-2 \Delta t) \gt 0$ :

Then, $\quad 1-2 \Delta t \leq 1$

$\Delta t \geq 0$

Case (ii) when $(1-2 \Delta t) \lt 0$ :

then $-(1-2 \Delta t) \leq 1$

$1-2 \Delta \mathrm{t} \geq-1$

$\Delta \mathrm{t} \leq 1$

$\therefore \quad$ Value of $\Delta t: 0 \leq \Delta t \leq 1$

pp:me:2024:q16.detailed_solution: Gerber Line. A parabolic curve joining $S_{e}$ on the ordinate to $S_{u t}$ on the abscissa is called the Gerber line. Soderberg Line A straight line joining $S_{e}$ on the ordinate to $\mathrm{S}_{\mathrm{yt}}$ on the abscissas called the Soderberg line. Goodman Line. A straight line joining $S_{e}$ on the ordinate to $S_{u t}$ on the abscissa is called the Goodman line. The Gerber parabola fits the failure points of test data in the best possible way. The goodman line fits beneath the scatter of this data. Both Gerber parabola and Goodman line intersect at $\left(\mathrm{S}_{\mathrm{e}}\right)$ on the ordinate to $\left(\mathrm{S}_{\mathrm{ut}}\right)$ on the abscissa. However, the Goodman line is more safe from design considerations because it is completely inside the Gerber parabola and inside the failure points. The Soderberg line is a more conservative failure criterion and there is no need to consider even yielding in this case.

pp:me:2024:q19.detailed_solution: Fig. Earning in a drawn steel cup, caused by the planar anisotropy of the sheet metal In deep drawing, the edges of cups may become wavy, called earing. Ears are objectionable on deep-drawn cups because they have to be trimmed off, as they serve no useful purpose, and interfere with further processing of the cup, resulting in scarp. Earing is caused by the planar anisotropy of the sheet metal, and the number of ears produced may be two, four or eight, depending on the processing history and microstructure of the material. If the sheet is stronger in the rolling direction than transverse to the rolling direction, and the strength varies uniformly with respect to orientation, then two ears will form. If the sheet has high strength at different orientations, then more ears will form.

pp:me:2024:q21.detailed_solution:
Types of allowances:

Draft/taper allowances.

Machining allowance/finishing allowance.

Distortion allowances/camber allowance

Shrinkage allowance/contraction allowances.

Shake allowance/rapping allowance.

Shake allowance

Before withdrawal from the sand mould, the pattern is wrapped all around the vertical faces to enlarge the mould cavity slightly, which facilitates its removal. Since it enlarge the final casting made, it is desirable that the original pattern dimensions should be reduced to account for this increase. There is no sure way of quantifying this allowance, since it is highly dependent on the foundry personnel and practices involved.

It is negative allowance and is to be applied only to those dimensions, which are parallel to the parting plane. One way of reducing this allowance is to increase the draft, which can be removed during the subsequent matching.

Draft/taper allowances

Once pattern is embedded in the moulding sand now it is required to withdrawing the pattern from moulding sand, for this propose a vertical force is required to lift the pattern. For easy removal of pattern from mould cavity there should be some degree or $\mathrm{mm}$ taper in the pattern.

If there is no taper in the pattern then more chance to break the mould cavity wall during withdrawing the pattern. Draft allowance varies with the complexity of job.

Machining or Finishing allowance

In sand casting operation machining/finishing allowances is given in the pattern as on solidification every metal get shrinked up to some extend and the outer surface of object (casting) is rough, therefore, to smoothing the outer surface of casting machining allowance is must.

Distortion allowance/Camber allowance

On just solidification of metal casting is weak, therefore, more chances to distorted casting. Chance of distortion are basically in $U, V$, then long section or complicated casting. Distortion can be minimized or eliminated by providing an allowance and constructed the pattern initially distorted, i.e. opposite in outer side direction. Among of distortion allowance varies from 1.5$20 \mathrm{~mm}$.

It is the tendency of all metals that they shrink after cooling except bismuth, Shrinkage is only due to inter atomic vibration which are implified by increasing in temperature. Metal shrink or contract in three ways :

Liquid Contraction

Solidification Contraction

Solid Contraction

pp:me:2025:q1.detailed_solution: Given: $A$ and $B$ are real symmetric matrices of the same size. Step 1: Understanding Symmetric Matrices A matrix $A$ is symmetric if: $A^T = A$ Similarly, $B$ is symmetric if: $B^T = B$ This property will help us evaluate the given options. Step 2: Evaluating the Given Options Option (A): $A^T = A^{-1}$ - This statement says that the transpose of $A$ is its inverse. - In general, a symmetric matrix $A$ satisfies $A^T = A$, but there is no guarantee that $A^T = A^{-1}$. - This is true only if $A$ is an **orthogonal matrix**, which is not given in the problem. - Thus, this statement is incorrect. Option (B): $AB = BA$ - In general, two symmetric matrices **do not necessarily commute**. - That is, $AB \ne BA$ in most cases. - Thus, this statement is incorrect. Option (C): $(AB)^T = B^T A^T$ - Using the property of transposition: $(AB)^T = B^T A^T$ - Since $A$ and $B$ are symmetric, we substitute $A^T = A$ and $B^T = B$: $(AB)^T = B A$ - This matches the given statement. - Thus, this statement is correct. ✅ Option (D): $A = A^{-1}$ - A matrix satisfying $A = A^{-1}$ is called an **involutory matrix**. - However, not all symmetric matrices satisfy this property. - The problem does not state that $A$ is involutory. - Thus, this statement is incorrect. Final Answer: The correct option is: $\boxed{(AB)^T = B^T A^T}$

pp:me:2025:q2.detailed_solution: Given: The differential equation: $\frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x^2} + \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial y^2} = 0$ for $0 \leq x \leq 1, 0 \leq y \leq 1$. Step 1: Understanding the Given Equation The given equation is the Laplace equation in two variables. A function $u(x, y)$ is a solution if its second partial derivatives sum to zero: $\frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x^2} + \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial y^2} = 0$. Step 2: Checking Each Option Option (A): $u = e^{x+y}$ First derivative: $\frac{\partial u}{\partial x} = e^{x+y}, \quad \frac{\partial u}{\partial y} = e^{x+y}$ Second derivative: $\frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x^2} = e^{x+y}, \quad \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial y^2} = e^{x+y}$ Summing them: $e^{x+y} + e^{x+y} = 2e^{x+y} \neq 0$ This is not a solution. Option (B): $u = e^x \sin y$ First derivatives: $\frac{\partial u}{\partial x} = e^x \sin y, \quad \frac{\partial u}{\partial y} = e^x \cos y$ Second derivatives: $\frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x^2} = e^x \sin y, \quad \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial y^2} = -e^x \sin y$ Summing them: $e^x \sin y - e^x \sin y = 0$ This is a valid solution. ✅ Option (C): $u = \sin x \sin y$ First derivatives: $\frac{\partial u}{\partial x} = \cos x \sin y, \quad \frac{\partial u}{\partial y} = \sin x \cos y$ Second derivatives: $\frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x^2} = -\sin x \sin y, \quad \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial y^2} = -\sin x \sin y$ Summing them: $-\sin x \sin y - \sin x \sin y = -2\sin x \sin y \neq 0$ This is not a solution. Option (D): $u = \cos x \cos y$ First derivatives: $\frac{\partial u}{\partial x} = -\sin x \cos y, \quad \frac{\partial u}{\partial y} = -\cos x \sin y$ Second derivatives: $\frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x^2} = -\cos x \cos y, \quad \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial y^2} = -\cos x \cos y$ Summing them: $-\cos x \cos y - \cos x \cos y = -2\cos x \cos y \neq 0$ This is not a solution. Final Answer: The correct option is: $\boxed{u = e^x \sin y}$ ✅

pp:me:2025:q3.detailed_solution: Given: The divergence of the curl of a vector field. Step 1: Understanding Curl and Divergence The curl of a vector field F, denoted as $\nabla \times \mathbf{F}$, results in another vector field. The divergence of a vector field G, denoted as $\nabla \cdot \mathbf{G}$, gives a scalar quantity. Step 2: Evaluating the Given Statement By a fundamental vector calculus identity: $\nabla \cdot (\nabla \times \mathbf{F}) = 0$ This states that the divergence of the curl of any vector field is always zero. Step 3: Checking the Given Options (A) The magnitude of this vector field → Incorrect, as the divergence of the curl is a scalar and always zero. (B) The argument of this vector field → Incorrect, as the divergence of the curl does not relate to an argument. (C) The magnitude of the curl of this vector field → Incorrect, as magnitude is not relevant to divergence. (D) Zero → Correct, as $\nabla \cdot (\nabla \times \mathbf{F}) = 0$. ✅ Final Answer: $\boxed{\text{Zero}}$

pp:me:2025:q6.detailed_solution: Step 1: Applying Torricelli’s Theorem The velocity of fluid exiting from the hole at the bottom of a tank is given by Torricelli’s theorem: $V = \sqrt{2 g h_{\text{eff}}}$ where: $V$ is the exit velocity $g$ is the acceleration due to gravity $h_{\text{eff}}$ is the effective height of the fluid column, which is given by: $h_{\text{eff}} = \frac{P_{\text{atm}}}{\rho g} + h$ Since both tanks are open to the atmosphere, the first term cancels out, leaving: $h_{\text{eff}} = h$ Thus, the velocity formula simplifies to: $V = \sqrt{2 g h}$ Step 2: Comparing Velocities for Water and Oil The exit velocity $V$ depends only on gravity and the height $h$. Since both tanks have the same $h$ and $g$, the exit velocity is independent of fluid density. Step 3: Checking the Given Options (A) $V_2 > V_1$ → Incorrect, because velocity does not depend on density. (B) $V_2 = V_1$ → Correct ✅ Both fluids have the same height and are in identical conditions. (C) $V_2 < V_1$ → Incorrect, as explained above. (D) Insufficient data → Incorrect, because Torricelli’s theorem provides a definite answer.

pp:me:2025:q7.detailed_solution: Step 1: Understanding the Froude Number Similarity In hydraulic modeling, the Froude number similarity is used when modeling free-surface flows such as river flow, scour, and waves. The Froude number is given by: $Fr = \frac{V}{\sqrt{g L}}$ where: - $V$ = velocity of flow - $g$ = acceleration due to gravity - $L$ = characteristic length (e.g., depth or length of the model) For dynamic similarity between a model and its prototype, the Froude number must be the same for both: $Fr_{\text{model}} = Fr_{\text{prototype}}$ Step 2: Setting Up the Equation $\frac{V_m}{\sqrt{g L_m}} = \frac{V_p}{\sqrt{g L_p}}$ Canceling $g$ on both sides: $\frac{V_m}{\sqrt{L_m}} = \frac{V_p}{\sqrt{L_p}}$ Rearrange for prototype velocity $V_p$: $V_p = V_m \times \sqrt{\frac{L_p}{L_m}}$ Given: - $\frac{L_p}{L_m} = 100$ - $V_m = 1$ m/s $V_p = 1 \times \sqrt{100} = 1 \times 10 = 10$ m/s

pp:me:2025:q9.detailed_solution: Step 1: Understanding the Psychrometric Chart A psychrometric chart is a graphical representation of air properties, commonly used in HVAC and thermodynamics. Step 3: Understanding Specific Humidity Specific humidity $\omega$ is defined as: $\omega = \frac{m_v}{m_a}$ where: $m_v$ = mass of water vapor (kg) $m_a$ = mass of dry air (kg) This represents the **mass of water vapor per unit mass of dry air**, making it a key parameter in psychrometric analysis. pp:me:2025:q12.detailed_solution: Given: The yield stress in uniaxial tension is $200, \text{MPa}$. We are to find the yield stress in pure shear according to the von Mises yield criterion. Step 1: Von Mises Yield Criterion in Terms of Shear The von Mises criterion relates the equivalent stress in a general stress state to the yield stress in uniaxial tension as: $\sigma_{\text{eq}} = \sqrt{\frac{3}{2} , \boldsymbol{s} : \boldsymbol{s}}$ In pure shear, the equivalent von Mises stress is: $\sigma_{\text{eq}} = \sqrt{3} , \tau$ where $\tau$ is the shear stress. Step 2: Set Equivalent Stress Equal to Yield Stress According to the von Mises criterion: $\sqrt{3} , \tau = 200$ Step 3: Solve for $\tau$ $\tau = \frac{200}{\sqrt{3}} \approx \frac{200}{1.732} \approx 115.47, \text{MPa}$

pp:me:2025:q15.detailed_solution: Given: Hole: $30^{+0.030}{+0.000} \ \text{mm}$ Shaft: $30^{+0.020}{-0.020} \ \text{mm}$ Step 1: Determine Maximum and Minimum Sizes Maximum Hole Size: $30 + 0.030 = 30.030 \ \text{mm}$ Minimum Hole Size: $30 + 0.000 = 30.000 \ \text{mm}$ Maximum Shaft Size: $30 + 0.020 = 30.020 \ \text{mm}$ Minimum Shaft Size: $30 - 0.020 = 29.980 \ \text{mm}$ Step 2: Calculate Possible Clearances Maximum Clearance: $30.030 - 29.980 = 0.050 \ \text{mm}$ Minimum Clearance: $30.000 - 30.020 = -0.020 \ \text{mm}$ (which is interference) Conclusion: Since the maximum clearance is positive and the minimum clearance is negative, the assembly may result in either a small clearance or interference. $\Rightarrow \text{This is a} \ \boxed{\text{transition fit}}$

pp:me:2025:q16.detailed_solution: Given: A rigid circular disc is rolling without slipping on a flat surface. Radius = $r$, Angular velocity = $\omega$ We are asked to find the velocities at points $O$ (center) and $A$ (bottom point of contact with ground). Step 1: Velocity of Center Point (O) For rolling without slipping, the center of the disc moves with linear velocity: $v_O = r \omega \hat{i}$ Step 2: Velocity of Point A (Point in contact with ground) Velocity of any point on a rotating body: $\vec{v} = \vec{v}_O + \vec{\omega} \times \vec{r}$ At point A, the rotational component is $-r \omega \hat{i}$ (due to clockwise rotation), and translational component is $r \omega \hat{i}$. So, $v_A = r\omega \hat{i} + (-r\omega \hat{i}) = 0 \hat{i}$ Final Answer: $\boxed{r\omega \hat{i} \ \text{and} \ 0 \hat{i}}$

pp:me:2025:q17.detailed_solution: Given: A truss is subjected to a horizontal load of $1000 \text{N}$ at point A. We need to identify the zero-force member among the given options: BD, BC, BA, AD. Step 1: Analyze Joint B At joint B, the following members are connected: • BA (inclined) • BC (inclined) • BD (horizontal) There is no external load or support at joint B. Therefore, the standard zero-force member rules cannot directly eliminate any member here. Step 2: Analyze Load Path The applied load $F = 1000 \text{N}$ is acting horizontally at point A. This load is transmitted from A to D (vertical support) and A to B. So, member BA will carry some force to maintain equilibrium at joint A. Step 3: Analyze Joint D At joint D, the following members are connected: • AD (vertical) • CD (horizontal) • BD (diagonal) Since support reactions are present at D, members AD and CD can balance vertical and horizontal loads respectively. There is no need for force to pass through BD to maintain equilibrium. Step 4: Conclusion As member BD does not contribute to the equilibrium of any joint and is not needed to transmit force: BD is a zero-force member. Final Answer: BD

pp:me:2025:q18.detailed_solution: Concept: In a hydrostatic stress condition, all normal stresses are equal in magnitude and compressive: $\sigma_x = \sigma_y = -P$ and $\tau_{xy} = 0$ Mohr's Circle Representation: Since there is no shear stress and both principal stresses are equal and negative: • The Mohr’s circle reduces to a point at $\sigma = -P$, $\tau = 0$ • Radius of Mohr’s circle = 0 (since $\sigma_1 = \sigma_2 = -P$) Analysis of Options: (A) Mohr’s circle centered at $P$ -> Incorrect, hydrostatic pressure causes compressive stress ($-P$) (B) Mohr’s circle centered at $-P$ with radius zero (a point) -> Correct (C) Circle with endpoints at $-P$ and $P$ -> Incorrect, implies unequal principal stresses (D) Circle with center at $0$, radius $P$ -> Incorrect

pp:me:2025:q19.detailed_solution: Concept: Balancing of rotating and reciprocating masses is essential in machines to reduce vibrations and improve performance and life. Rotating Masses: Rotating masses can be balanced by adding counter masses. A rigid rotor unbalanced in space (not just in one plane) needs to be balanced in both magnitude and direction in 3D. Reciprocating Masses: Reciprocating masses (like in single-cylinder IC engines) cannot be perfectly balanced because of the nature of reciprocating motion—only partial balancing is possible. Step 1: For a rigid rotor, full dynamic balance (i.e., both force and couple balance) requires placing two balancing masses in two distinct planes. So, option (A) is incorrect—a single balancing mass cannot balance both force and couple. Step 2: A single-cylinder engine produces unbalanced reciprocating inertia forces. It is not possible to completely balance all forces and couples with just masses. Hence, options (C) and (D) are incorrect. Final Answer: ✅ Correct option: (B)

pp:me:2025:q20.detailed_solution: Given: A shaft carries a helical spur gear. Concept: Helical gears produce three types of forces: radial, axial (thrust), and tangential forces due to the angled teeth. Therefore, the bearing used must be capable of handling both radial and axial loads. Option (A): Angular contact bearing Can handle both radial and axial loads. Hence, it is suitable for supporting a helical gear. Option (B): Double-row ball bearing Can support higher radial loads and some axial loads in both directions. Hence, suitable for helical gears. Option (C): Straight roller bearing Can support only radial loads and not axial loads. Hence, it is not suitable for helical gears which produce axial thrust. Option (D): Tapered roller bearing Can support both radial and axial loads. Hence, suitable for helical gears.

pp:me:2025:q21.detailed_solution: Given: The values of the function $f(x)$ at different $x$ are: $$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|} \hline x & 0 & 0.25 & 0.5 & 0.75 & 1.0 \\ \hline f(x) & 0.9 & 2.0 & 1.5 & 1.8 & 0.4 \\ \hline \end{array}$$ We will apply Simpson’s 1/3 Rule: $\int_{a}^{b} f(x), dx \approx \frac{h}{3} \left[ f(x_0) + 4(f(x_1) + f(x_3)) + 2(f(x_2)) + f(x_4) \right]$ Here, $h = \frac{1 - 0}{4} = 0.25$ Substituting values: $\int_0^1 f(x),dx \approx \frac{0.25}{3} \left[ 0.9 + 4(2.0 + 1.8) + 2(1.5) + 0.4 \right]$ $= \frac{0.25}{3} \left[ 0.9 + 4(3.8) + 3.0 + 0.4 \right]$ $= \frac{0.25}{3} \times (0.9 + 15.2 + 3.0 + 0.4) = \frac{0.25}{3} \times 19.5$ $= \frac{4.875}{3} = 1.625$ Final Answer: $\boxed{1.63}$ (rounded to 2 decimal places)

pp:me:2025:q22.detailed_solution: Given: Thermal efficiency of Otto cycle $\eta = 0.5$ Specific heat ratio of air $\gamma = 1.4$ We are to find the compression ratio $r$. Step 1: The efficiency of an ideal Otto cycle is given by: $\eta = 1 - \dfrac{1}{r^{\gamma - 1}}$ Step 2: Substitute the known values: $0.5 = 1 - \dfrac{1}{r^{1.4 - 1}} = 1 - \dfrac{1}{r^{0.4}}$ Rearranging: $\dfrac{1}{r^{0.4}} = 0.5$ $r^{0.4} = 2$ Step 3: Raise both sides to the power $\dfrac{1}{0.4} = 2.5$: $r = 2^{2.5} = \sqrt{2^5} = \sqrt{32} \approx 5.657$ Final Answer: $\boxed{5.7}$ (rounded off to 1 decimal place)

pp:me:2025:q23.detailed_solution: Given: Total incident power = $2500\ \text{W}$ 85% of power is absorbed within a circle of radius $R = 5\ \text{mm}$ 65% of power is absorbed within an inner circle of radius $r = 3\ \text{mm}$ We are to find the power density in the shaded area (annular region between 3 mm and 5 mm) Step 1: Calculate absorbed powers $P_{5} = 0.85 \times 2500 = 2125\ \text{W}$ $P_{3} = 0.65 \times 2500 = 1625\ \text{W}$ Step 2: Power absorbed in the shaded annular area $P_{\text{shaded}} = P_5 - P_3 = 2125 - 1625 = 500\ \text{W}$ Step 3: Area of shaded region = Area of outer circle – Area of inner circle $A = \pi (R^2 - r^2) = \pi (5^2 - 3^2) = \pi (25 - 9) = \pi \times 16 \approx 50.27\ \text{mm}^2$ Step 4: Power density $\text{Power Density} = \dfrac{P_{\text{shaded}}}{A} = \dfrac{500}{50.27} \approx 9.95\ \text{W/mm}^2$

pp:me:2025:q24.detailed_solution: Given: Initial size of the cube: $200\ \text{mm} \times 200\ \text{mm} \times 200\ \text{mm}$ Volumetric shrinkage during solidification: $7%$ Volumetric shrinkage during solid contraction: $8%$ Shrinkage occurs in volume, but we are asked about the final edge length assuming uniform cooling in all directions. Step 1: Total volumetric shrinkage $V_{\text{initial}} = 200^3 = 8,000,000\ \text{mm}^3$ After solidification (7% shrinkage): $V_1 = V_{\text{initial}} \times (1 - 0.07) = 8,000,000 \times 0.93 = 7,440,000\ \text{mm}^3$ After solid contraction (8% shrinkage): $V_2 = V_1 \times (1 - 0.08) = 7,440,000 \times 0.92 = 6,844,800\ \text{mm}^3$ Step 2: Final volume is a cube, so $L^3 = 6,844,800$ $L = \sqrt[3]{6,844,800} \approx 188.0\ \text{mm}$

pp:me:2025:q25.detailed_solution: Given: Mass of the block, $m = 1\ \text{kg}$ Spring stiffness, $k = 10\ \text{N/m}$ It is given that the damping ratio $\zeta$ is equal to the ratio of damped frequency to natural frequency: $\zeta = \dfrac{\omega_d}{\omega_n}$ Step 1: Natural frequency $\omega_n = \sqrt{\dfrac{k}{m}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{10}{1}} = \sqrt{10}$ Step 2: Relation between damped and natural frequency $\omega_d = \omega_n \sqrt{1 - \zeta^2}$ Substitute into the given condition: $\zeta = \dfrac{\omega_d}{\omega_n} = \sqrt{1 - \zeta^2}$ Step 3: Solve the equation Square both sides: $\zeta^2 = 1 - \zeta^2$ $2\zeta^2 = 1$ $\zeta^2 = \dfrac{1}{2}$ $\zeta = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \approx 0.71$

pp:me:2025:q26.detailed_solution: Given: $f(x) = 2x^3 - 9x^2 + 12x$ over the closed interval [0, 3] Step 1: Find the derivative $f'(x)$ to get critical points $f'(x) = \dfrac{d}{dx}(2x^3 - 9x^2 + 12x) = 6x^2 - 18x + 12$ Step 2: Set $f'(x) = 0$ and solve for $x$ $6x^2 - 18x + 12 = 0$ Divide entire equation by 6: $x^2 - 3x + 2 = 0$ $(x - 1)(x - 2) = 0$ So, critical points are $x = 1$ and $x = 2$ Step 3: Evaluate $f(x)$ at endpoints and critical points $f(0) = 2(0)^3 - 9(0)^2 + 12(0) = 0$ $f(1) = 2(1)^3 - 9(1)^2 + 12(1) = 2 - 9 + 12 = 5$ $f(2) = 2(8) - 9(4) + 12(2) = 16 - 36 + 24 = 4$ $f(3) = 2(27) - 9(9) + 12(3) = 54 - 81 + 36 = 9$ Step 4: Find the minimum value among these $\min{0,\ 4,\ 5,\ 9} = 0$

pp:me:2025:q27.detailed_solution: Given: Actual and forecast demand for 10 periods is provided. We are to compute: Mean Forecast Error (MFE): average of (Actual - Forecast) Mean Absolute Deviation (MAD): average of |Actual - Forecast| Step 1: Create a table of differences: $$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|} \hline \text{Period} & \text{Actual} & \text{Forecast} & \text{Error} = A - F & |\text{Error}| \\ \hline 1 & 425 & 427 & -2 & 2 \\ 2 & 415 & 422 & -7 & 7 \\ 3 & 420 & 416 & 4 & 4 \\ 4 & 430 & 422 & 8 & 8 \\ 5 & 427 & 423 & 4 & 4 \\ 6 & 418 & 420 & -2 & 2 \\ 7 & 422 & 419 & 3 & 3 \\ 8 & 416 & 418 & -2 & 2 \\ 9 & 426 & 430 & -4 & 4 \\ 10 & 421 & 415 & 6 & 6 \\ \hline \text{Total} & - & - & 8 & 42 \\ \hline \end{array}$$ Step 2: Compute MFE and MAD $\text{MFE} = \frac{\sum (A - F)}{10} = \frac{8}{10} = 0.8$ $\text{MAD} = \frac{\sum |A - F|}{10} = \frac{42}{10} = 4.2$ Final Answer: Mean Forecast Error = $0.8$ Mean Absolute Deviation = $4.2$

pp:me:2025:q28.detailed_solution: Given: We need to match mold elements with their correct functions in the casting process. Let’s go through each mold element: P. pp:me:2025:q32.detailed_solution: Step 1: Stiffness of Cantilever Beam The stiffness of a cantilever beam with flexural rigidity $EI$ and length $L$ is: $k_{\text{beam}} = \frac{3EI}{L^3}$ Step 2: Total Equivalent Stiffness The spring (stiffness $K$) and the beam act in parallel, so the total stiffness is the sum: $k_{\text{total}} = \frac{3EI}{L^3} + K$ Step 3: Natural Frequency Formula For a lumped mass-spring system, the natural frequency is given by: $\omega_n = \sqrt{\frac{k_{\text{total}}}{m}}$ Substituting the expression for total stiffness: $\omega_n = \sqrt{\frac{\frac{3EI}{L^3} + K}{m}}$ Final Answer: $\boxed{\omega_n = \sqrt{\frac{\frac{3EI}{L^3} + K}{m}}}$

pp:me:2025:q33.detailed_solution: Given: Endurance limit = Yield strength = $\sigma_y$ Ultimate strength = $2\sigma_y$ Factor of safety (FOS) = 2 Loading is fully tensile and periodic (i.e., reversed loading) Life requirement: at least $10^6$ cycles → high-cycle fatigue Use Soderberg criterion for design Step 1: Soderberg Equation The Soderberg criterion is: $\frac{\sigma_a}{\sigma_e} + \frac{\sigma_m}{\sigma_y} \leq \frac{1}{\text{FOS}}$ Where: $\sigma_a$ = alternating stress = $\frac{\sigma_{\text{max}} - \sigma_{\text{min}}}{2}$ $\sigma_m$ = mean stress = $\frac{\sigma_{\text{max}} + \sigma_{\text{min}}}{2}$ For fully reversed loading: $\sigma_{\text{min}} = 0$, so: $\sigma_a = \sigma_m = \frac{\sigma_{\text{max}}}{2}$ Step 2: Substitute in Soderberg equation $\frac{\sigma_{\text{max}}/2}{\sigma_e} + \frac{\sigma_{\text{max}}/2}{\sigma_y} \leq \frac{1}{2}$ Since $\sigma_e = \sigma_y$, both terms are equal: $\frac{\sigma_{\text{max}}}{2\sigma_y} + \frac{\sigma_{\text{max}}}{2\sigma_y} = \frac{\sigma_{\text{max}}}{\sigma_y}$ Step 3: Apply Soderberg Limit $\frac{\sigma_{\text{max}}}{\sigma_y} \leq \frac{1}{2}$ So, $\sigma_{\text{max}} \leq \frac{\sigma_y}{2}$ Step 4: Relate to Endurance Limit Since $\sigma_y = \sigma_e$, $\sigma_{\text{max}} \leq \frac{\sigma_e}{2}$ Final Answer: $\boxed{\text{The maximum applied tensile principal stress is half of the endurance limit}}$
